newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Exporter says Argentine cotton hard hit by drought.
newsitem.headline: Exporter says Argentine cotton hard hit by drought.

text.p: Argentina's 1996/97 cotton crop was badly hit by drought earlier this year, stripping output of as much as 100,000 tonnes of lint, a top cotton exporter said Monday.

With harvesting about 40 percent complete, the extent of the damage has become clear and final lint output is likely to total about 300,000 tonnes, Rafael Almiroty, of Almiroty y Compania, told Reuters.

"There was drought and a lot of heat all through January and up to the beginning of February," he said. "There was patchy rain in February, which we thought would alleviate the problems, but the months passed and the crops were harder hit by the drought than we thought."
Unusually late sowing meant that the plants were still very small when drought struck, and more vulnerable to heat stress.

Almiroty warned that still more damage could be done to the crop if there are early frosts, although so far the harvesting weather has been pleasingly warm and dry. Harvesting is likely to be over by June.

Disappointing output should mean Argentina will only export about 200,000 tonnes of cotton lint, with the rest feeding the anaemic local textile industry. Most of this lint has already been sold in advance, mainly to Brazil, Almiroty said.

Recent dry weather has meant that cotton quality is generally fairly good, and has not suffered nearly as much as yield. There was some damage due to ill-timed rain in Santiago del Estero, but most of the crop in the crucial zone of Chaco province was not spoilt, Almiroty said.
Farmers sowed over 900,000 hectares with cotton, down from a record 1.0 million hectares in 1995/96 but still well above the historical average. Last year's lint output was 425,000 tonnes.
While this season's yields have been bad, farmers are likely to be tempted by high cotton prices to sow another big cotton area in 1997/98, Almiroty said.
Argentine farmers have invested heavily in cotton farming in recent years, and now the vast majority of the crop is harvested by machine instead of being picked by hand.
